title: OpenAI rolls out GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast — 8× faster, 6× price, in Codex and the API
subtitle: The paid speed tier for GPT-6.1 Sol lands in ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API at $12 input and $60 output per million tokens, limited to Pro 500 and eligible enterprise or education accounts.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI began rolling out GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast on October 9. The tier delivers the same model that launched at DevDay 2026, but served at up to 8× the standard latency, at a price of $12 per million input tokens and $60 per million output tokens — 6× the posted Sol rates. Access is available through the API as the model id gpt-6.1-sol-ultrafast and inside Codex and ChatGPT Work for Pro 500 accounts, eligible usage-based Enterprise plans, and credit-based Edu accounts. Cached input stays at the base Sol rate. OpenAI notes the 8× figure is a ceiling, not a floor — real workloads will fall somewhere between standard Sol and the ceiling depending on prompt shape.

The mechanism matters more than the speed-up itself. Ultrafast is the first production tier where OpenAI explicitly separates latency from capability — same weights, same evals, different serving infrastructure. For agentic workloads where the model is in a tight loop with a tool server, cutting end-to-end latency by a factor of two to eight collapses the wall-clock cost of long chains, even at 6× the per-token price. For human-in-the-loop coding, it changes whether a Codex session feels like a conversation or a wait. Pricing roughly matches the Astra-era premium ratio, which argues OpenAI sees Ultrafast as a durable tier rather than a promotional launch.

This slots neatly into the DevDay 2026 arc — Sol priced to match frontier open-weights, Luna held back on cyber grounds, Astra on the retire path — and against competitors it is the clearest answer yet to Google's Gemini production-tier push and Anthropic's cache-read discounts on Sonnet 5.5. The read on the market is that developers now have three stacked choices from the same lab for one model family: cheap, fast, and both. The question of whether Ultrafast serves the same quality under load as Standard will be answered by third-party arena runs over the next few weeks.

For learners: when a model stays the same but the serving changes, that is where the engineering lives. Try Ultrafast on a workload you already run on Sol Standard and measure three things — p50 latency, p99 latency, and tokens per output. Do not assume 8×; measure. If your agent spends more time waiting for tool calls than for the model, Ultrafast will not help you much and you will overpay. If your agent is in a tight model-tool loop, it will change the shape of what you can build. The lesson generalizes — infrastructure choices are now part of the model you ship.
